A hillside is viewed from the side, with arrows showing where rain runs down the slope, where it collects in a low place, and where it soaks in where the ground is flat.
Understanding water movement: where rain goes on your land

Before you harvest water, learn where it already goes. Watch from a safe place during heavy rain. When it is safe afterwards, walk your land. Look for rills (small water channels), places where water spreads, where it collects, and where it leaves your land. Some excess water needs a safe path to travel away so that it does not cause damage.

An A-frame level (a tool shaped like the letter A that helps find places of equal height) can help you mark points at the same height and follow a contour line. Its marks are observation only; they are not a plan or permission for earthworks. Before digging a swale (a trench for catching water along a contour line), a dam or another structure, ask for your site to be assessed. Soil, slope, drainage, heavy-rain flow and a safe outlet for excess water all matter. Ask a trained local adviser.

There is no single placement rule followed on all slopes. Look where water moves and collects. Badly placed contour lines can increase soil erosion, and soil that absorbs water slowly can hold too much water. Choose any water works that suit your site and plan a safe path for excess water.

back: Sun position, shade and aspect: using sunlight well

In many parts of South Africa, especially in winter, the sun is in the north. Its path changes with the season and with location. North-facing slopes usually get more sun and can be hotter and drier. South-facing slopes usually stay cooler and moister. Frost can collect in low places where cold air settles. Check your site yourself before choosing where to plant tender plants or put buildings.

The winter sun is lower and further north than the summer sun. A wall or shade cloth can shade a bed for longer in winter than in summer. Before placing anything long-lasting, stand at that spot at 8am, at noon and at 4pm on a winter day and see where the shade falls.

Pawpaw and young citrus trees (fruit trees) are sensitive to frost. Keep tender plants away from known low places where frost collects. Check local frost before planting.

Wind, frost and landform: reading invisible forces

Wind can damage plants on a small farm. The direction and strength of damaging wind change by region, by season, and with the ridges and gaps of your site. Walk your land on windy days. Record where the wind comes from and what it [typo verb] affects. Check local weather records before deciding where shelter is needed.

On clear, still nights, cold air can flow down the slope and collect in low places. These places can be colder than the surrounding slopes. Frost patterns also depend on the site. Compare the spots you might choose during the local frost season. Check local minimum-temperature records where they exist. If records do not exist, keep watching on cold nights and ask a local agricultural adviser before choosing a permanent home for tender young plants (seedlings).

Frost is ice that forms on a cold surface. Mist/fog alone does not show that ice has formed, and frost damage can happen without visible ice. Look for ice and plant damage, compare low ground and slopes, and check minimum temperature where you can. Note places where cold or damage lasts long. Keep sensitive plants away from the cold places you have seen.

For tomato with a late blight problem (a tomato plant disease), air movement and morning sun can help leaves dry. Late blight can still spread during long cool, damp weather. Moving the bed BUT will not control it; also seek local plant-health guidance.

Making a simple site map: your design starts on paper

A site map needs paper, a measuring tape, a compass and time to walk your land. Walk the boundary and make a first drawing. Label it 'not measured' until you check its distances. Mark north. Add the house, trees, water, paths and fences. Draw arrows for summer and winter wind, shade paths, and where water flows when it rains.

Note where frost stays long, where the soil SMELLS of wetness in the dry months, and where khakibos or blackjack grows densely. These plants can grow in disturbed places, but their presence BUT does not show whether the soil is compacted. Test the soil before deciding what that place means for your design.

Put your zones and sectors over the same drawing. Update it every season. A pencil drawing you really use is worth more than a perfect one made once.

Seed and seed sovereignty (control of seed)
Save, store and share seed — freedom from buying seed every season.
Two seed packets above a simple comparison: five plants that look alike on the left and five different plants on the right. The real offspring depends on the variety and on pollination.
Why saving seed matters

Open-pollinated seed from a stable variety can produce similar plants when pollination (the transfer of pollen from one flower to another) is properly managed. F1 hybrids come from selected parents. Their saved seed may germinate, but the next generation varies; it may not keep the combination you wanted.

Seed sovereignty includes the knowledge and choice needed to plant, save and share suitable seed. Keep the plant identity and variety with each batch of seed.

Choose healthy plants with useful traits. Start with a crop you know, and ask a seed-saving adviser how to manage its pollination and selection.

back: How to save seed: dry and wet methods

Dry seed must ripen before it is collected. Remove the chaff (soft rubbish around the seed) and damaged seed, then finish drying it in the shade with moving air.

Seed in fleshy fruit needs a specific method for each crop. Tomato seed can be 'fertilised/rotted' (fermented) for a short time to help remove its gel, then cleaned and dried well. Keep the working jar open or loosely covered. Fermentation is not needed for all wet-seeded crops and does not guarantee disease-free seed.

Pollination (the transfer of pollen from one flower to another) also matters. Maize is 'brought in' by the wind and can cross with other varieties. Tomatoes mostly pollinate themselves, but crossing happens. Check the crop and variety before planning isolation or seed saving.

back: Drying, storing and sharing seed

Dry seed well before storing it: in paper envelopes, not plastic, in a shaded place with moving air — never use direct sun or enclosed heat. The three enemies of a seed's ability to germinate are heat, light and moisture. Seed life in storage varies by crop and conditions, so test germination before relying on stored seed.

Write on each envelope the crop, variety and date it was saved. Keep well-dried seed in a sealed container in a cool, dark, dry place. Sealing wet seed can STOP moisture and spoil it.

Before a new planting season, test a small batch for germination so that you do not rely on seed that has quietly lost its ability to germinate.

Plan a seed swap with neighbours this season. What one household saves well, many households can share — and the variety diversity of the whole group grows with each swap.
